query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, the addition of a modest amount (~5 at.%) of Al—as opposed to equivalent additions of Mn or Si—reduces the outward cation diffusion rates (especially of Cr and Mn) at temperatures above 900 °C, thereby favoring the in situ formation of a thin, coherent, and adherent mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3 protective oxide layer. In contrast, Mn or Si additions do not sufficiently slow diffusion, so these alloys develop thicker, porous oxide scales that crack or spall.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase CrFeCoNi base alloy with controlled grain size, modified separately by ~5 at.% addition of either Al, Mn, or Si, and a baseline sample with no extra addition.
generation.intervention: Expose all alloy variants to an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere (e.g., 20% O2/80% N2 with trace Na2SO4) at temperatures between 900 °C and 1100 °C for extended durations (e.g., 24 to 100 hours).
generation.conditions: Isothermal high-temperature exposure in a controlled reactive atmosphere ensuring consistent oxygen partial pressure and presence of corrosive species; the alloys must be processed to yield single-phase microstructures so that the effect of the alloying element is isolated.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of the oxide scale is mediated by the diffusion kinetics of key cations at the alloy/oxide interface. In the Al-doped alloy, higher activation energy for Cr (and competing Mn) diffusion reduces rapid cation outflow, allowing formation of a conformal, thin composite oxide. In Mn- or Si-doped alloys, faster cation flux fosters the formation of thicker, non-uniform oxide layers prone to pore development and spallation.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum in the alloy increases the energy barrier for outward diffusion of active cations, thus maintaining a balanced flux between oxygen inward diffusion and metal cation supply. This restricted cation mobility leads to a uniform, adherent layer predominantly composed of Al2O3 in combination with Cr2O3. Conversely, Mn or Si does not sufficiently impede cation diffusion, resulting in excessive cation supply at the surface, leading to thicker, porous oxides that experience tensile stress and eventual cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions, only the Al-doped CrFeCoNi alloy will form and maintain a stable, thin (on the order of ~1 µm or less), coherent protective oxide scale with minimal spallation. The Mn-doped and Si-doped variants (and the baseline) will develop thicker, less uniform oxide layers that show pronounced cracking, pore formation, and spallation.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior of the unmodified single-phase CrFeCoNi alloy (or its previously documented behavior with layered Mn- and Cr-oxides) serves as the baseline for comparison to evaluate the effect of adding Al, Mn, or Si.
generation.boundary: These results are expected to hold for samples processed to be fully single-phase with controlled grain size and homogeneity, and for exposures above 900 °C in environments with similar oxygen partial pressures and corrosive species. The hypothesis may not directly extend to multiphase or highly segregated microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g., PMC9692591 on Al-content effects and PMC10384371 on Mn-driven oxide evolution) provide evidence on separate roles of Al and Mn in oxide formation, the specific impact of Si in this system is underexplored. The combined study under identical high-temperature, corrosive conditions and in a single-phase microstructure is novel; uncertainties remain regarding exact diffusion activation energies and the quantitative scale thickness differences, particularly for Si-modified alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of single-phase CrFeCoNi alloys: one baseline, one with 5 at.% Al, one with 5 at.% Mn, and one with 5 at.% Si. Subject all samples to isothermal oxidation in a controlled atmosphere (20% O2/80% N2 with trace Na2SO4) at 1000 °C for 50 hours. Use in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) to monitor oxide phase evolution and post-exposure cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and atom probe tomography (APT) to characterize oxide scale thickness, homogeneity, composition, and spallation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Phase composition and distribution (via XRD and EDS mapping)
Quantification of oxide spallation (area fraction or mass loss measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a significantly thinner, more coherent, and adherent oxide scale (e.g., with minimal spallation and a scale thickness <~1 µm) compared to the Mn- and Si-doped alloys and the baseline, then the hypothesis that Al specifically retards cation diffusion to form a stable protective oxide scale is falsified. Alternatively, if Mn- or Si-doped alloys also form similarly stable oxide scales, the mechanistic distinction being proposed would be invalid.

The oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA provides valuable insights into its suitability for high-temperature applications. This oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi HEA plays a critical role in determining its mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties in elevated temperature environments. The observed non-protective oxide formation, particularly the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy, can have significant implications for this particular alloy’s mechanical properties. Mn is known to contribute to solid solution strengthening and can enhance the mechanical strength and ductility of alloys. Therefore, the formation of non-protective oxides and the depletion of Mn may negatively affect the mechanical performance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA at high temperatures.

The oxidation behavior of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA produced by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C up to 48 h. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The initial alloy was verified as FCC random solid solution. The mass gain in the oxidation process for 48 h was measured to be 0.02 and 0.15 g/cm2 at 700 °C and 900 °C, respectively. (2) MnFe2O4, MnFeO2 and Cr2O3 were detected by the XRD analysis on the specimen surface. Some surface cracks were observed, especially for those oxidized at 900 °C. The spallation of oxide layer took place when the alloy was tested at 900 °C. The high-temperature oxidation resistance of the alloy sharply decreased when the test temperature increased from 700 °C to 900 °C, leading to the wide application under 700 °C.

Chen et al. investigated the effect of Si (0.3 atom %) content on the oxidation behavior of the Al0.6CrFeCoNi HEA and found that the oxidation kinetics of the Si-containing HEA was lower than that of the Al0.6CrFeCoNi HEA at lower temperatures (800 and 900 °C) but became inferior compared to Al0.6CrFeCoNi at the higher temperature of 1000 °C. Lu et al. reported the effect of Al content on the oxidation behavior of Y/Hf-doped AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.7, 1, 1.3) high-entropy alloys. Al0.7CoCrFeNi showed the lowest oxidation resistance owing to the formation of an outer spinel layer with an inner Al2O3 layer, followed by AlCoCrFeNi due to the formation of protective Al2O3 scale and Al1.3CoCrFeNi exhibiting the highest resistance to oxidation. While the major focus of prior studies has been on the development of new alloy systems, there are only a few studies on limiting the high temperature oxidation via tailoring the material’s microstructure. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
